steps.label: Do Now: Fetching a Value (1 of 2)
steps.content:
Do Now: Fetching a Value (1 of 2)

Recap of 3.1.2 to 3.1.4. Cambridge IGCSE 0478/12, June 2026, Question 2(c). What to do: type your answer, then press Check my answer or Submit answer.

A computer has a central processing unit (CPU). The memory address register (MAR) and the memory data register (MDR) are two registers built into the CPU.

items.prompt: A value is fetched from random access memory (RAM) to the CPU. Explain how the MAR and MDR are used in this process.
scheme: The MAR stores the address or location of the value // the address is sent or copied to the MAR ...
... the address of the value or data that is to be fetched, in RAM
The MDR stores the value or data // the value or data is sent or copied to the MDR
items.guidance: Three from the points, one mark each. Point 2 follows on from point 1. Points 2 and 3: benefit of the doubt for instruction in place of value or data.
items.modelAnswer: The address of the value in RAM is sent to the MAR. The value at that address is sent to the MDR.

walkthrough.title: Walk me through it: how two parts are used

steps.text: A similar question. "Two numbers are added in the CPU. Explain how the ALU and the ACC are used." It is worth 3 marks.
Take one part at a time. What does the ALU do in this process? It carries out the addition.
Now the ACC: what does it hold, and which one? It stores the result of the addition.
A third point is the detail: which thing it is, or where it comes from. "The result is stored in the ACC, ready for the next calculation."
steps.visual: what it does + what it holds + which one

steps.text: Now your question. Take the MAR, then the MDR. For each one: what does it hold in this fetch, and where does that come from?
steps.visual: MAR: what? MDR: what? where from?

steps.label: Do Now: Inside the CPU (2 of 2)
steps.content:
Do Now: Inside the CPU (2 of 2)

Recap of 3.1.2. Cambridge IGCSE 0478/13, November 2023, Question 3(a) (adapted: typed, not circled). A computer has a central processing unit (CPU). What to do: type your answer, then press Check my answer or Submit answer.

items.prompt: (a) Type the three components that are built into the CPU: accumulator (ACC), control unit (CU), graphics card, hard disk drive (HDD), motherboard, program counter (PC), random access memory (RAM), read only memory (ROM).
scheme: Accumulator (ACC)
Control unit (CU)
Program counter (PC)
items.guidance: One mark for each correct component. Online the components are typed instead of circled: if more than three are given, mark only the first three.

walkthrough.title: Walk me through it: inside the CPU or not?

steps.text: A similar question. "Circle two components that are not built into the CPU: ALU, keyboard, MAR, printer, CIR."
steps.visual: ask the same question about every item

steps.text: For each item ask: is it a register or a unit that the CPU uses to run instructions? Those are built into the CPU.
steps.visual: register or unit? inside the CPU

steps.text: ALU: a unit, inside. MAR: a register, inside. CIR: a register, inside.
Keyboard and printer: devices joined to the computer, outside the CPU. So the answer is keyboard and printer.
Now your list. Which three are registers or units inside the CPU? The others are cards, disks or memory outside it.

steps.label: Extension: Do Now Challenge
steps.content:
Extension: Do Now Challenge

Extension: finished the Do Now? Try these questions on the fetch-decode-execute cycle. Pick the answer that earns the mark, then type it. Stuck? Switch on I need help. Go to the next slide when you are ready.

steps.label: CPU Performance
steps.content:
3.1 Computer Architecture

CPU Performance

Year 10

  • Today: three things inside a CPU that make it run programs faster, and why each one works.
  • Small numbers all lesson: two CPUs, one task, which finishes first?
  • How this lesson works: on each slide, read the facts, predict by picking an answer, then read why.
Think → Pair → ShareTwo computers open the same game. One opens it sooner. Predict: what could be different inside the faster one?Show the answer

Ideas to collect: it carries out more instructions each second, it waits less for data, it works on more than one thing at once. Today tests each idea.

steps.label: Why One CPU Finishes First
steps.content:
Why One CPU Finishes First

What to do: read the facts, then pick your prediction. The reason appears under it.

  • CPU A and CPU B run the same program: 12 instructions.
CPU A
3 instructions a second
CPU B
6 instructions a second
Think → Pair → ShareWhy do people care how fast a computer runs a program?Show the answer

Programs open and respond sooner, games run smoothly, and big jobs such as video finish in less time.

items.prompt: Predict: which CPU finishes the program first?
items.explain: B: 12 ÷ 6 = 2 seconds. A: 12 ÷ 3 = 4 seconds. How fast a CPU carries out instructions is its performance. Better performance: programs finish sooner.

steps.label: The Clock: One Cycle Each Pulse
steps.content:
The Clock: One Cycle Each Pulse

What to do: read the facts, then pick your prediction. The reason appears under it.

  • Inside the CPU is a clock. It sends out pulses, one after another.
  • On each pulse, the CPU carries out one FDE cycle: one instruction is fetched, decoded and executed.
pulse pulse pulse pulse pulse

5 pulses = 5 FDE cycles = 5 instructions

items.prompt: Predict: a tiny CPU's clock sends 5 pulses each second. How long does a program of 20 instructions take?
items.explain: One instruction on each pulse, 5 pulses a second: 5 instructions a second. 20 ÷ 5 = 4 seconds.

steps.label: Clock Speed and GHz
steps.content:
Clock Speed and GHz

What to do: read the facts, then pick your prediction. The reason appears under it.

  • Clock speed: the number of FDE cycles the CPU carries out in one second.
  • It is measured in hertz (Hz): 1 Hz is 1 cycle a second.
  • 1 GHz (gigahertz) is 1 billion cycles a second.

items.prompt: Predict: a CPU has a clock speed of 3.2 GHz. How many FDE cycles does it carry out in one second?
items.explain: G means billion. 3.2 GHz is 3.2 billion FDE cycles every second, so up to 3.2 billion instructions every second.

steps.label: Compare: 2 GHz and 4 GHz
steps.content:
Compare: 2 GHz and 4 GHz

What to do: compare the two CPUs, then pick your prediction. The reason appears under it.

  • Both CPUs run the same program: 8 billion instructions.
  • Everything else about them is the same.
CPU A: 2 GHz
2 billion FDE cycles a second
CPU B: 4 GHz
4 billion FDE cycles a second

items.prompt: Predict: how long does each CPU take?
items.explain: A: 8 ÷ 2 = 4 seconds. B: 8 ÷ 4 = 2 seconds. A higher clock speed means more FDE cycles each second, so more instructions are processed each second: better performance.

steps.label: Your Notes: Clock Speed
steps.content:
Your Notes: Clock Speed

What to do: open your notes (the notepad button at the top) and write each note in your own words. Then press Check my note and compare. Fix your note if it misses an idea.

Note in your notes: explain what a clock speed of 3 GHz means.Check my note

A model note: 3 billion FDE cycles each second. So up to 3 billion instructions can be processed each second.

Note in your notes: explain WHY a higher clock speed can improve performance.Check my note

A model note: More FDE cycles happen each second, so more instructions are processed each second. Programs finish sooner.

steps.label: Exam Question: Clock Speed (1 of 2)
steps.content:
Exam Question: Clock Speed (1 of 2)

Cambridge IGCSE 0478/12, November 2023, Question 3(a)(i). A user's computer has a central processing unit (CPU) that has a clock speed of 2 GHz. She wants to change it to a CPU that has a clock speed of 3 GHz. What to do: type your answer, then press Check my answer or Submit answer.

items.prompt: (i) State what is meant by clock speed.
scheme: The (maximum) number of FDE cycles or instructions a CPU can perform, process or execute in a second
items.guidance: One mark. It must say per second (or a second). "How fast the CPU is" earns no mark.
items.modelAnswer: The number of FDE cycles the CPU can carry out in a second.

steps.label: Exam Question: Clock Speed (2 of 2)
steps.content:
Exam Question: Clock Speed (2 of 2)

Cambridge IGCSE 0478/12, November 2023, Question 3(a)(ii). A user's computer has a central processing unit (CPU) that has a clock speed of 2 GHz. She wants to change it to a CPU that has a clock speed of 3 GHz. What to do: type your answer, then press Check my answer or Submit answer.

items.prompt: (ii) Explain the effect this change will have on the performance of the CPU.
scheme: It increases or improves the performance // tasks can be performed quicker or faster
... because more FDE cycles or instructions can be processed in a second
items.guidance: Two from the points, one mark each. Point 2 follows on from point 1.
items.modelAnswer: It improves the performance, because more FDE cycles can be processed in a second.

steps.label: Why the CPU Waits for RAM
steps.content:
Why the CPU Waits for RAM

What to do: read the facts, then pick your prediction. The reason appears under it.

  • Instructions and data are stored in RAM, outside the CPU.
  • RAM is much slower than the CPU. Each fetch from RAM makes the CPU wait.

items.prompt: Predict: a game uses the same picture data again and again. How could the CPU wait less?
options: Keep a copy of that data close, inside the CPU
Fetch it from RAM more often
items.explain: Keep a copy close. A small, fast memory inside the CPU (or very near it) holds frequently used data and instructions. It is called cache. Cache is faster to access than RAM, so the CPU waits less.

steps.label: Compare: A Small Cache and a Big Cache
steps.content:
Compare: A Small Cache and a Big Cache

What to do: compare the two CPUs, then pick your prediction. The reason appears under it.

  • Both CPUs run the same game. It uses 6 MB of data again and again.
CPU A: 2 MB cache
3 GHz
CPU B: 8 MB cache
3 GHz

items.prompt: Predict: which CPU runs the game faster, and why?
options: B: all 6 MB fits in its cache, so it waits less for RAM
A: a small cache is quicker to fill
Neither: the clock speeds are the same
items.explain: 6 MB fits in B's cache but not in A's, so A keeps fetching data from the slower RAM. More cache: more frequently used data is found quickly, so performance improves.

steps.label: Exam Question: The Purpose of Cache (1 of 2)
steps.content:
Exam Question: The Purpose of Cache (1 of 2)

Cambridge IGCSE 0478/13, November 2025, Question 2(c)(i). The computer has primary storage. One example of primary storage is cache. What to do: pick one statement.

items.prompt: Tick one box to show the correct statement that describes the purpose of cache.
options: It stores the next instruction to be processed.
It stores instructions so they are not lost when the power is turned off.
items.explain: Cache stores frequently used instructions (and data), so the CPU finds them quickly without waiting for RAM.

steps.label: Exam Question: The Purpose of Cache (2 of 2)
steps.content:
Exam Question: The Purpose of Cache (2 of 2)

Cambridge IGCSE 0478/13, November 2023, Question 3(b). A computer has a central processing unit (CPU). The CPU has cache. What to do: type your answer, then press Check my answer or Submit answer.

items.prompt: (b) Explain the purpose of the cache.
scheme: It is a type of storage ...
... that stores frequently used data or instructions
To speed up access ...
... as it is faster to access than RAM
It has different levels, for example L1 to L3
items.guidance: Any two from the points, one mark each. A point marked ... follows on from the point before it.
items.modelAnswer: It stores frequently used data, because it is faster to access than RAM.

steps.label: Your Notes: Cache
steps.content:
Your Notes: Cache

What to do: open your notes (the notepad button at the top) and write each note in your own words. Then press Check my note and compare. Fix your note if it misses an idea.

Note in your notes: explain what cache is.Check my note

A model note: Small, fast memory inside or near the CPU. It holds frequently used data and instructions.

Note in your notes: explain WHY more cache can improve performance.Check my note

A model note: More frequently used data and instructions can be stored in it. They are found quickly, so the CPU waits less for the slower RAM.

steps.label: More Than One Core
steps.content:
More Than One Core

What to do: read the facts, then pick your prediction. The reason appears under it.

  • So far each CPU had one CU, one ALU and one set of registers, running one FDE cycle at a time. One set like this is a core.
  • A dual-core CPU has 2 cores. A quad-core CPU has 4. Each core runs its own FDE cycle at the same time.
CPU
Core 1
CU, ALU, registers
its own FDE cycle
Core 2
CU, ALU, registers
its own FDE cycle

items.prompt: Predict: a dual-core CPU has a clock speed of 2 GHz. How many instructions can it process in one second?
items.explain: Each core: 2 billion instructions a second. Both cores work at the same time: 2 + 2 = 4 billion a second.

steps.label: Compare: 1 Core and 4 Cores
steps.content:
Compare: 1 Core and 4 Cores

What to do: compare the two CPUs, then pick your prediction. The reason appears under it.

  • The task: edit 4 photos, 12 billion instructions.
  • It can be split: each core edits one photo.
CPU A: 1 core
3 GHz
CPU B: 4 cores
3 GHz

items.prompt: Predict: how long does each CPU take?
items.explain: A: 12 ÷ 3 = 4 seconds. B: 4 cores × 3 billion = 12 billion a second, so 12 ÷ 12 = 1 second. More cores: more instructions are processed at the same time.

steps.label: Compare: A Task That Cannot Be Split
steps.content:
Compare: A Task That Cannot Be Split

What to do: compare the two CPUs, then pick your prediction. The reason appears under it.

  • A new task: a calculation of 12 billion steps.
  • Each step needs the answer from the step before, so it cannot be split.
CPU A: 1 core
3 GHz
CPU B: 4 cores
3 GHz

items.prompt: Predict: how long does each CPU take now?
items.explain: Only one core can work on it, so the other three wait. Both take 12 ÷ 3 = 4 seconds. More cores only help if a task can be split. Cores must also communicate with each other, which takes time, so 4 cores are not always 4 times as fast.

steps.label: Your Notes: Cores
steps.content:
Your Notes: Cores

What to do: open your notes (the notepad button at the top) and write each note in your own words. Then press Check my note and compare. Fix your note if it misses an idea.

Note in your notes: explain what a core is.Check my note

A model note: A processing unit inside the CPU. It runs its own FDE cycle: it fetches, decodes and executes instructions.

Note in your notes: explain WHY more cores can improve performance.Check my note

A model note: Each core processes its own instructions at the same time, so more instructions are processed at once.

Note in your notes: explain WHY more cores do not always help.Check my note

A model note: Some tasks cannot be split, so only one core works on them. The cores also have to communicate, which takes time.

steps.content:
Exam Question: Cores (1 of 2)

Cambridge IGCSE 0478/13, June 2023, Question 2(a). A library has a self-checkout system. The self-checkout system has a central processing unit (CPU). The CPU has two cores. What to do: type your answer, then press Check my answer or Submit answer.

items.prompt: (a) State the purpose of a core in the CPU.
scheme: To perform a fetch-decode-execute cycle // to process or execute an instruction

steps.label: Exam Question: Cores (2 of 2)
steps.content:
Exam Question: Cores (2 of 2)

Cambridge IGCSE 0478/13, June 2023, Question 2(b). A library has a self-checkout system. The self-checkout system has a central processing unit (CPU). The CPU has two cores. What to do: type your answer, then press Check my answer or Submit answer.

items.prompt: (b) The CPU is replaced with one that has four cores. Explain the effect this has on the performance of the self-checkout system.
scheme: It may increase the performance
... because more instructions can be processed simultaneously
items.guidance: Two from the points, one mark each. Point 2 follows on from point 1.
items.modelAnswer: It may increase the performance, because more instructions can be processed at the same time.

steps.label: Check: Which Change Helps?
steps.content:
Check: Which Change Helps?

What to do: pick the change that helps each task. Ask: can the task be split? Is the CPU waiting for RAM? Done when both are answered.

items.prompt: A photo app keeps fetching the same 6 MB of data from RAM. The CPU has 2 MB of cache, and most of its time is spent waiting. Which change helps most?
items.explain: A bigger cache. With 8 MB of cache the 6 MB of data fits, so the CPU stops waiting for RAM.

items.prompt: A task cannot be split. Which change makes it finish sooner?
items.explain: A higher clock speed: more FDE cycles each second on the one core that works on it. Extra cores would have nothing to do.

steps.label: Activity 1: CPU Race
steps.content:
Activity 1: CPU Race

What to do: two CPUs race on the same task. Level 1: pick which finishes first, and why. Level 2: type how many seconds each one takes, then pick. One check per round, and a mistake means the round does not count. Done when you have cleared level 2 (two clean rounds in a row at each level). The help gets less as you go up.

scheme: C has a higher clock speed // B has at most 5 GHz in total

What to do: now read each task carefully: can it be split, and does its data fit in the cache? Type how long each CPU takes. At level 4, pick the best upgrade for one CPU and type its new time. A mistake means the round does not count. Done when you have cleared level 4, with no help.

steps.label: Exam Question: Why a Different CPU Can Be Faster
steps.content:
Exam Question: Why a Different CPU Can Be Faster

Cambridge IGCSE 0478/13, June 2024, Question 8(d). A student has a computer that has a central processing unit (CPU). What to do: type your answer, then press Check my answer or Submit answer.

items.prompt: (d) The student wants to replace the CPU to increase the performance of the computer. Explain why a different CPU can increase the performance.
scheme: It could have more cores
... increasing the number of FDE cycles or instructions it can perform at the same time
It could have a higher clock speed
... increasing the number of FDE cycles or instructions per second it can perform
It could have a greater cache size
... meaning more frequently used data can be accessed faster
items.guidance: Any four from the points, one mark each. A point marked ... follows on from the point before it.
items.modelAnswer: It could have more cores, so more instructions are performed at the same time. It could have a higher clock speed, so more FDE cycles are performed per second.
